statement: To construct a cube and comprehend it in a sphere, like the pyramid; and to prove that the square on the diameter of the sphere is triple of the square on the side of the cube.
heath_proof: Let the diameter AB of the given sphere be set out, and let it be cut at C so that AC is double of CB; let the semicircle ADB be described on AB, let CD be drawn from C at right angles to AB, and let DB be joined; let the square EFGH having its side equal to DB be set out, from E, F, G, H let EK, FL, GM, HN be drawn at right angles to the plane of the square EFGH, from EK, FL, GM, HN let EK, FL, GM, HN respectively be cut off equal to one of the straight lines EF, FG, GH, HE, and let KL, LM, MN, NK be joined; therefore the cube FN has been constructed which is contained by six equal squares. It is then required to comprehend it in the given sphere, and to prove that the square on the diameter of the sphere is triple of the square on the side of the cube. For let KG, EG be joined. Then, since the angle KEG is right, because KE is also at right angles to the plane EG and of course to the straight line EG also, [XI. Def. 3] therefore the semicircle described on KG will also pass through the point E. Again, since GF is at right angles to each of the straight lines FL, FE, GF is also at right angles to the plane FK; hence also, if we join FK, GF will be at right angles to FK; and for this reason again the semicircle described on GK will also pass through F. Similarly it will also pass through the remaining angular points of the cube. If then, KG remaining fixed, the semicircle be carried round and restored to the same position from which it began to be moved, the cube will be comprehended in a sphere. I say next that it is also comprehended in the given sphere. For, since GF is equal to FE, and the angle at F is right, therefore the square on EG is double of the square on EF. But EF is equal to EK; therefore the square on EG is double of the square on EK; hence the squares on GE, EK, that is the square on GK [I. 47], is triple of the square on EK. And, since AB is triple of BC, while, as AB is to BC, so is the square on AB to the square on BD, therefore the square on AB is triple of the square on BD. But the square on GK was also proved triple of the square on KE. And KE was made equal to DB; therefore KG is also equal to AB. And AB is the diameter of the given sphere; therefore KG is also equal to the diameter of the given sphere. Therefore the cube has been comprehended in the given sphere; and it has been demonstrated at the same time that the square on the diameter of the sphere is triple of the square on the side of the cube.

13.15
**Statement:** To construct a cube and comprehend it in a sphere, like the pyramid; and to prove that the square on the diameter of the sphere is triple of the square on the side of the cube.

**Step 1.** Let AB be the diameter of the given sphere. Cut off from AB a third part CB [6.9]; then AB is triple of CB, and the remainder AC is double of CB.

**Step 2.** Bisect AB at O [1.10]; with centre O and distance OA describe a circle [P3]; the part of it on one side of the diameter AB is the semicircle ADB [D1.18]. From C draw CD at right angles to AB [1.11], meeting the circumference at D, and join DB [P1].

**Step 3.** The angle ADB, being an angle in the semicircle ADB, is right [3.31]. Thus ADB is a right-angled triangle, and DC is the perpendicular drawn from the right angle to the base AB; therefore the triangle DBC is similar to the whole triangle ABD, and, the sides about the common angle at B being proportional, AB : BD = BD : BC [6.8].

**Step 4.** Since AB, BD, BC are three proportional straight lines, AB has to BC the ratio duplicate of that which AB has to BD [D5.9]. But the square on AB has to the square on BD the ratio duplicate of that which AB has to BD, the two squares being similar rectilineal figures [6.20]. Therefore, as AB is to BC, so is the square on AB to the square on BD [5.11]. And AB is triple of BC (Step 1); therefore the square on AB is triple of the square on BD [D5.5].

**Step 5.** Let a straight line EF be taken equal to DB [1.3], and on EF let the square EFGH be described [1.46]. From the points E, F, G, H let EK, FL, GM, HN be set up at right angles to the plane of the square EFGH [11.12], and let EK, FL, GM, HN be cut off each equal to EF [1.3]. Join KL, LM, MN, NK [P1].

**Step 6.** Since EK and FL are both at right angles to the same plane EFGH, EK is parallel to FL [11.6]; hence E, F, L, K lie in one plane [D1.23]. Moreover EK = FL, and KL joins their extremities in the same direction; therefore KL is equal and parallel to EF [1.33]. In the same way FL is parallel to GM, GM to HN, and HN to EK [11.6], and LM is equal and parallel to FG, MN to GH, and NK to HE [1.33].

**Step 7.** In the plane quadrilateral EFLK the four sides EF, FL, LK, KE are all equal to EF (Steps 5, 6), so it is equilateral. Since EK is at right angles to the plane EFGH, it makes a right angle with EF, which lies in that plane [D11.3]; so the angle KEF is right, and likewise the angle EFL is right, FL being at right angles to the same plane [D11.3]. Since KL is parallel to EF and EK falls on them, the angles EKL, KEF together equal two right angles [1.29], so that the angle EKL is right; and since FL falls on the same parallels, the angle KLF is right likewise [1.29]. Therefore EFLK is equilateral and right-angled, that is, a square [D1.22], and it is equal to the square EFGH, its side being equal to EF. In the same way FGML, GHNM, HEKN are squares equal to EFGH.

**Step 8.** KL is parallel to EF and MN to GH (Step 6), and EF is parallel to GH, because the angles EFG, FGH of the square are together equal to two right angles [1.28]; these straight lines not being all in one plane, KL is parallel to GH, and hence KL is parallel to MN [11.9]. Therefore K, L, M, N lie in one plane [D1.23]. The sides KL, LM, MN, NK are equal to EF, FG, GH, HE respectively (Step 6), hence all equal, so KLMN is equilateral. Again, LK, LM meeting at L are parallel respectively to FE, FG meeting at F, and the two pairs are not in the same plane; therefore the angle KLM is equal to the angle EFG [11.10], which is right. Similarly the angles LMN, MNK, NKL are right. Hence KLMN is a square [D1.22] equal to EFGH.

**Step 9.** Therefore the solid figure bounded by EFGH, KLMN, EFLK, FGML, GHNM, HEKN is contained by six equal squares, and so it is a cube [D11.25]; its side EF is equal to DB.

**Step 10.** Join KG and EG [P1]. Since KE is at right angles to the plane EFGH and EG lies in that plane, the angle KEG is right [D11.3]. Therefore the semicircle described on KG in the plane of K, E, G passes through E; for the angle in a semicircle is right [3.31].

**Step 11.** Again, GF is at right angles to FE, the angle EFG of the square being right, and also to FL, since FL is at right angles to the plane EFGH in which GF lies [D11.3]; and FE, FL cut one another at F. Therefore GF is at right angles to the plane through FE, FL, that is, the plane of the square EFLK [11.4]. Join FK [P1]; FK, joining points on the parallels EK, FL, lies in that plane [11.7]; therefore GF is at right angles to FK [D11.3], and the angle KFG is right. Hence the semicircle described on KG in the plane of K, F, G passes through F [3.31].

**Step 12.** In the same way GH, being at right angles to HE and to HN, is at right angles to the plane of the square HEKN [11.4], in which HK lies [11.7], so that the angle KHG is right. KL, being at right angles to LF and to LM (Steps 7, 8), is at right angles to the plane of the square FGML [11.4], in which LG lies [11.7], so that the angle KLG is right; likewise KN is at right angles to the plane of the square GHNM, in which NG lies, so that the angle KNG is right. Lastly, since EK and GM are equal and parallel, KM is equal and parallel to EG [1.33]; GM makes a right angle with GE, which lies in the plane EFGH [D11.3]; and since KM is parallel to EG and GM falls on them, the angles KMG, MGE together equal two right angles [1.29], so that the angle KMG is right. Therefore the semicircles described on KG in the planes of KHG, KLG, KNG, KMG pass through H, L, N, M respectively [3.31].

**Step 13.** If then, KG remaining fixed, the semicircle described on KG be carried round and restored to the same position from which it began to be moved, the figure so comprehended is a sphere [D11.14], of which KG is a diameter [D11.17]. In its revolution the semicircle passes through each of the points E, F, H, L, M, N (Steps 10-12), while K and G are the extremities of the diameter; hence all eight angular points of the cube lie on the surface of this sphere, and the cube is comprehended in it.

**Step 14.** Since the angle EFG is right, the square on EG is equal to the squares on EF, FG [1.47], that is, to double the square on EF, because FG is equal to EF. And since the angle KEG is right (Step 10), the square on KG is equal to the squares on KE, EG [1.47]; and KE is equal to EF; therefore the square on KG is triple of the square on EF.

**Step 15.** But EF is equal to DB (Step 5), so that the square on EF is equal to the square on DB; therefore the square on KG is triple of the square on DB. And the square on AB is triple of the square on DB (Step 4). Therefore the square on KG is equal to the square on AB [CN1], and KG is equal to AB. Thus the diameter KG of the sphere comprehending the cube is equal to the diameter AB of the given sphere, so that this sphere is equal to the given sphere; therefore the cube has been comprehended in the given sphere.

**Step 16.** Finally, the square on AB, the diameter of the sphere, is equal to the square on KG, which is triple of the square on EF, the side of the cube (Step 14). Therefore a cube has been constructed and comprehended in the given sphere, and the square on the diameter of the sphere is triple of the square on the side of the cube. Q.E.F.
